blocks.text: In sp³ hybridization, one s-orbital (low energy and spherical) and three p-orbitals (high energy and dumbbell shaped), intermix to give a new set of four orbitals of same energy and same shape. Each of these hybrid orbitals is a sp³ hybrid orbital. These hybrid orbitals are arranged in the tetrahedral geometry as shown in the example of CH₄ as in Fig. 3.27.
The electronic configurations of valence shell of ₆C in its excited and hybridized states are given as follows:

blocks.alt: Orbital boxes for carbon in three rows. 6C ground: 2s with a pair of opposite arrows, 2px and 2py with one up arrow each, 2pz empty (Ground). C excited: 2s, 2px, 2py and 2pz each with one up arrow (Excited). C hybridized: four sp3 boxes each with one up arrow (hybridized).
blocks.caption: Electron boxes of carbon in the ground, excited and sp3 hybridized states (original drawing after the box diagrams printed in the textbook).

blocks.text: The energies of hybrid orbitals are lower than unhybrid orbitals. Figure 3.27 shows the outermost four atomic orbitals of carbon mix up to give four hybrid orbitals of same energy and same shape.

blocks.alt: Top: a 2s orbital (sphere with +) plus a 2px, a 2py and a 2pz orbital, each a dumb-bell on x, y and z axes with one outlined lobe marked +. Bottom: 'Shape of one sp3 orbital having two lobes', a small and a large lobe, and 'Four sp3 hybrid orbitals', four lobes pointing to the corners of a tetrahedron.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.27: Formation of sp3 hybrid orbitals of C in methane (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 3.27).

blocks.title: Did you Know?
blocks.text: Each sp³ hybrid orbital consists of two lobes, one larger and the other smaller. For the sake of simplicity, the smaller lobe is usually not shown while representing sp³ hybrid orbitals together.

The four new hybrid orbitals of equal energy have a tetrahedral geometry with carbon nucleus at the center. The methane molecule is formed by the overlap of sp³ hybrid orbitals of carbon with 1s orbitals of four hydrogen atoms separately to form four sigma bonds. The four C-H bonds, which result from sp³-s overlaps, are directed towards the corners of a regular tetrahedron.

In sp² hybridization, one s and two p atomic orbitals of an atom intermix to form three orbitals called sp² hybrid orbitals. The three half-filled sp² hybrid orbitals are arranged in a trigonal planar geometry with bond angles of 120°.

blocks.alt: A 2s orbital plus a 2px orbital plus a 2py orbital on axes, an arrow labelled 'Hybridization', and three sp2 lobes in a plane with a curved double arrow labelled 120 degrees. Below right: 'Shape of one sp2 orbital', a small lobe marked + and a large lobe.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.29: Formation of sp2 hybrid orbitals from atomic orbitals (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 3.29).

blocks.text: The sp² hybridization explains the geometry of planar molecules such as BF₃. Electronic configuration of ₅B is:

blocks.alt: Orbital boxes for boron in three rows. 5B ground: 2s with a pair of opposite arrows, 2px with one up arrow, 2py and 2pz empty. B excited: 2s, 2px and 2py each with one up arrow, 2pz empty. B hybridized: three sp2 boxes each with one up arrow.
blocks.caption: Electron boxes of boron in the ground, excited and sp2 hybridized states (original drawing after the box diagrams printed in the textbook).

blocks.text: The three outermost orbitals of B mix together to give three sp² hybrid orbitals. On the other hand, one of the p orbitals of fluorine is half filled (e.g. 2pz). BF₃ is formed by the overlap of three half-filled sp² hybrid orbitals of boron with 2pz orbitals of three fluorine atoms. The structure is triangular planar with bond angles equal to 120°, each.

blocks.alt: (a) A boron atom with three brown sp2 lobes at 120 degrees, each overlapping the blue 2pz orbital of a fluorine atom; labels sp2, F and 2pz. (b) The line drawing of BF3: B bonded to three F atoms, a dotted triangle joining the F atoms, and an angle of 120 degrees.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.30: Formation of BF3 molecule through sp2-p overlap (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 3.30).

blocks.text: In sp hybridization, one s (low energy and spherical) and one p orbital (high energy and dumb-bell shaped), intermix to give a new set of two orbitals of same energy and same shape called sp hybrid orbitals. These sp hybrid orbitals are arranged in linear geometry and oriented at 180°. The electronic configuration of the outermost shell of Be is as follows:

blocks.alt: Orbital boxes for beryllium in three rows. 4Be ground: 2s with a pair of opposite arrows, all three 2p boxes empty. Be excited: 2s and 2px with one up arrow each, 2py and 2pz empty. Be hybridized: two sp boxes each with one up arrow.
blocks.caption: Electron boxes of beryllium in the ground, excited and sp hybridized states (original drawing after the box diagrams printed in the textbook).

blocks.text: The two sp hybrid orbitals lie linearly as in the following diagram Fig. 3.32. The sp hybridization explains the geometry of linear molecules such as beryllium chloride, BeCl₂. It is formed when two sp hybrid orbitals of Be atom overlap with the half-filled p-orbitals of chlorine atoms.

blocks.alt: Top: an s orbital plus a p orbital, an arrow labelled 'Hybridization', 'Two sp hybrid orbitals' pointing opposite ways, and 'sp hybrid orbitals shown together (Large lobes only)'. Bottom: Cl p orbitals overlapping the two sp lobes of Be in a line, with 180 degrees marked, equal to Cl-Be-Cl with 180 degrees.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.32: Mixing of s and p orbitals to give two hybrid sp orbitals and the formation of BeCl2 (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 3.32).
